name: Vitamin K cream

card.summary: Topical vitamin K, marketed for vascular-type dark circles and bruising; popular in eye-care marketing but with little evidence behind it in our sources.
card.note: Vitamin K's established medical roles are systemic; benefits for dark circles are not established in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Vitamin K creams are cosmetic products containing vitamin K (usually K1, phylloquinone), sold with claims that they reduce the bluish or purplish look of under-eye circles and bruising.

The theory is that dark circles from visible blood vessels or small leaks of blood pigment can fade if vitamin K supports clotting locally. This theory has not been established by the sources consulted here.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin K acts systemically as a cofactor for enzymes that make clotting proteins functional. Proponents of topical use extend this to the skin; whether topical application changes under-eye blood vessels or pigment is not shown in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Orally, no toxicity has been documented for K1 or K2 and no upper limits are set. Intravenous K1 has caused rare severe allergic-type reactions. Cosmetic creams can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.

lead: Vitamin K cream is a cosmetic product containing vitamin K, usually phylloquinone (K1), marketed for dark circles with a vascular component and for bruising. Vitamin K is a family of fat-soluble vitamins; its recognised medical uses are systemic, such as preventing bleeding in newborns and reversing excess warfarin effect [1].

Dark circles have multiple causes, including pigmentation, thin skin that shows underlying vessels, allergy and nutritional factors; a cream targeting only one mechanism may affect only some presentations [2]. The sources reviewed did not describe topical vitamin K as an established treatment for dark circles.

paras: Henrik Dam found in 1929 that chicks fed a fat-depleted diet bled, and proposed a missing coagulation factor; the letter K derives from the German word for coagulation. Dam and Edward Doisy shared the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work [1].
The vitamin is a cofactor in making clotting proteins such as prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X functional [1].

Eye products containing vitamin K are marketed for under-eye discoloration. The idea relied on in marketing is that clotting-related support could reduce blood pooling or leakage that shows through thin skin; this rationale is a hypothesis in the material reviewed, and general references on dark circles discuss other treatments, such as caffeine, vitamin C, lasers and fillers, rather than vitamin K [2].

High oral intakes of K1 and K2 have no known toxicity and regulators in the US, Japan and the EU have not set upper limits. Intravenous K1 can cause serious anaphylactoid reactions in about 3 per 10,000 treatments, mostly linked to a castor-oil solubilizer. Synthetic menadione (K3) was banned as a supplement in the US because of allergic reactions and hemolytic anemia [1]. These figures concern systemic use, not cosmetic creams.

timeline.event: Henrik Dam reports a dietary factor needed for blood coagulation, later named vitamin K. [1]
Dam and Edward Doisy share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on vitamin K. [1]
